exhibits.title: Settling Down
exhibits.change: Hunter-gatherers built stone houses and stayed year-round — before farming.
exhibits.context: Natufian communities in the Levant lived in round, semi-subterranean houses, harvested wild cereals with sickles, buried their dead within settlements and kept dogs. Sedentism came before domesticated crops, not after.
exhibits.significance: Permanent villages created the conditions — storage, population growth, attachment to place — in which farming could take hold.

exhibits.title: The Oldest Bread
exhibits.change: Charred flatbread crumbs from a hunter-gatherer hearth.
exhibits.context: Charred food remains in a fireplace at Shubayqa 1 were identified in 2018 as flatbread-like products made from wild cereals and club-rush tubers, about 4,000 years before farming.
exhibits.significance: Labour-intensive processing of wild grains may have been one of the incentives to cultivate them.

exhibits.title: Göbekli Tepe
exhibits.change: Monumental carved pillars, raised by people who had not yet fully domesticated plants or animals.
exhibits.context: Circular enclosures with T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 metres tall, carved with foxes, snakes, vultures and human arms. Excavation continues to change interpretations: once seen purely as a ritual centre, it is now understood to have had domestic occupation too.
exhibits.significance: Large-scale cooperation and monumental building came at the very start of the Neolithic, not only after it.

uncertainty.note: Its function and the degree of settlement are still debated.

exhibits.title: Agriculture

when.display: from c. 9500 BCE — invented independently in several regions

regions.note: Fertile Crescent: wheat, barley, lentil, pea (c. 9500–7500 BCE).
Potato, quinoa, squash; llama and alpaca.
Sorghum and pearl millet in the Sahel.

exhibits.change: Humans began to shape plants and animals — and were reshaped by them.
exhibits.context: Domestication happened independently in at least seven to eleven regions, often gradually over thousands of years. Selection by harvesters produced crops that kept their seeds on the stalk and grew larger grains. Farming supported far denser populations, but early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than foragers.
exhibits.significance: Surplus food made villages, specialists, cities, states and writing possible — and began humanity's reshaping of Earth's ecosystems.

uncertainty.note: The number of independent centres, and why farming arose at roughly the same time in several places after the Ice Age, are debated.

exhibits.title: Founder Crops

regions.note: Einkorn traced genetically to the Karacadağ hills.

exhibits.change: Emmer, einkorn, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax.
exhibits.context: These eight 'founder crops' were domesticated across the Fertile Crescent over roughly two thousand years. Domestic traits — non-shattering ears, larger seeds — spread slowly through wild-type populations.
exhibits.significance: The crop package that later spread with farmers into Europe, North Africa and South Asia.

exhibits.title: Mud Brick
exhibits.change: Shaped, sun-dried earth: a building block anyone could make.
exhibits.context: Hand-formed bricks appear in early Neolithic Jericho; mould-made bricks later allowed standard sizes. Mud brick became the building material of Mesopotamian and Egyptian cities.
exhibits.significance: A modular unit of construction — the basis of the first cities.

exhibits.title: Hammered Copper

regions.note: Native copper tools, from several millennia BCE.

exhibits.change: Native copper was hammered and annealed into beads, awls and pins.
exhibits.context: Early farmers in southeastern Anatolia cold-hammered naturally occurring copper and learned that heating it (annealing) stopped it becoming brittle. Around the Great Lakes, a separate tradition worked native copper into tools.
exhibits.significance: The first metal — worked before anyone could smelt ore.

exhibits.title: Herding

when.display: sheep, goats, cattle and pigs from c. 8500 BCE; independently elsewhere

exhibits.change: Animals were kept, bred and managed rather than hunted.
exhibits.context: Changes in size, age-at-death patterns and DNA show domestic sheep and goats by about 8500 BCE in the northern Fertile Crescent. Cattle were domesticated at least twice (Near East and South Asia) and pigs independently in Anatolia and China.
exhibits.significance: Meat, milk, wool and — later — muscle power for ploughs and carts. Close contact also brought new diseases.

exhibits.title: Clay Tokens
exhibits.change: Small clay shapes stood for measures of grain, oil and livestock.
exhibits.context: Cones, spheres and discs of clay appear across the Near East from early farming times. Later they were sealed inside clay envelopes marked on the outside — a step many scholars link to the invention of writing.
exhibits.significance: Recording quantities outside the head: the administrative seed of writing and accounting.

uncertainty.note: The direct token-to-writing pathway proposed by Denise Schmandt-Besserat is influential but debated in its details.

exhibits.title: The Walls of Jericho
exhibits.change: A stone wall and an 8-metre tower around an early farming settlement.
exhibits.context: Pre-Pottery Neolithic Jericho was surrounded by a stone wall with a massive round tower with an internal staircase. Whether they defended against people or against floods is debated.
exhibits.significance: Organised communal building on a new scale.

exhibits.title: Millet on the Yellow River
exhibits.change: Broomcorn and foxtail millet became the grain of northern China.
exhibits.context: Storage pits at Cishan contained large quantities of millet. Millet farming in northern China developed independently of Near Eastern farming.
exhibits.significance: The agricultural foundation of the Yellow River civilisations.

exhibits.title: Woven Cloth

when.display: fibre-working by c. 30,000 years ago; woven cloth by c. 8000–7000 BCE

exhibits.change: Threads interlaced on a frame became flexible, strong fabric.
exhibits.context: Dyed flax fibres from Dzudzuana suggest string-making tens of thousands of years ago. Twined and woven textiles survive from about 8000–7000 BCE in the Levant, and independently from early Andean caves.
exhibits.significance: Cloth for clothing, sails, bags and nets; the loom later inspired punched-card programming.

uncertainty.note: Textiles rarely survive, so their origins are surely older.

exhibits.title: Çatalhöyük
exhibits.change: Thousands of people lived in packed houses entered through the roof.
exhibits.context: Houses were built wall-to-wall without streets, with painted plaster and burials beneath floors. Evidence suggests a relatively egalitarian society without obvious palaces or temples.
exhibits.significance: Large-scale settled life before cities or states.

exhibits.title: Maize
exhibits.change: A wild grass with a few hard kernels became the cob that fed the Americas.
exhibits.context: Genetics identifies Balsas teosinte as maize's wild ancestor, and starch grains at Xihuatoxtla show maize processing about 8,700 years ago. Squash was domesticated even earlier in Mexico. Maize changed profoundly over millennia of selection.
exhibits.significance: Maize supported Mesoamerican and later North American societies and today is one of the world's most important crops.

sources.note: Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS; Matsuoka et al. 2002.

exhibits.title: Rice in the Yangtze

when.display: cultivated by c. 7000 BCE; fully domesticated over millennia

exhibits.change: Wetland rice, gathered and then cultivated, became a staple.
exhibits.context: Rice use is attested at Shangshan sites from about 9000 BCE; managed cultivation developed over the following millennia, with fully domesticated rice established by about 5000–4000 BCE.
exhibits.significance: Rice now feeds more people than any other grain.

uncertainty.note: The pace of domestication and possible additional domestications in South Asia are debated.

exhibits.title: Kuk Swamp Gardens

when.display: from c. 7000 BCE; mounded fields by c. 5000 BCE

exhibits.change: Drained plots in the New Guinea highlands for taro, banana and yam.
exhibits.context: Ditches, mounds and plant remains show that highland New Guineans began cultivating plants independently, with drainage systems developing over millennia.
exhibits.significance: One of the clearest independent inventions of agriculture — and bananas later spread across the tropics.

sources.note: Denham et al. 2003, Science. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

exhibits.title: Mehrgarh
exhibits.change: One of South Asia's earliest farming villages — with drilled teeth.
exhibits.context: Mehrgarh's farmers grew barley and wheat and herded zebu cattle. Several molars from about 7000–5500 BCE show holes drilled with flint bits: among the earliest evidence of dentistry.
exhibits.significance: The deep background of the Indus civilisation.

exhibits.title: Irrigation
exhibits.change: Channels carried river water to fields that rain could not feed.
exhibits.context: Canals at Choga Mami in eastern Iraq date to the Samarran period. Irrigation let farming spread onto the dry plains of southern Mesopotamia, where the first cities would grow. Andean farmers developed irrigation independently.
exhibits.significance: Water management required cooperation and organisation — a root of administration and the state.

exhibits.title: The Kiln
exhibits.change: A chamber that trapped heat and separated fire from the pots.
exhibits.context: Updraft kilns reached higher, more even temperatures than open firing, producing harder, more consistent ceramics. Temperature control learned in kilns underlies later smelting.
exhibits.significance: Controlled high temperature — the gateway to metal and glass.
